about: Ganda (Ghent): the two abbeys where the Leie meets the Scheldt, 793 to 1066. Written 6 Oct 2026 from Design/content/dossiers/ganda.md and the spine (threads godfreds_market, price_of_england, hungry_years, book_road). A draft for the user to overwrite. Other files already name ganda.cellarer, ganda.einhard and the site ganda.abbey: they are kept here under those ids.

ports.summary: Ganda in 793 is not a town: two of the king's abbeys and a village on the river bank, where the Leie runs into the Scheldt in several arms. Saint Bavo's stands at the meeting of the waters and Saint Peter's on the sand hill of Blandinium upstream; canons serve both, serfs and tenants work their land, and boats lie on the Scheldt's left bank between the abbey and the village. A merchant comes because the abbeys gather wool, cheese, cloth and dues from estates as far as the sea and must send them on, because wax and good silver are always wanted here, and because the bank has wrights who can mend a hull.
ports.seasons: The Leie meadows lie under water for part of every winter and are sheep ground when they dry; shearing is before Saint John's day. The year's great day is Saint Bavo's Mass on the first of October, when the dues come in, the abbot's men ride home and every bench on the bank is taken. Saint Veerle is kept on the fourth day after the new year and Saint Amand in the first week of February, when the river is often too high to bring a boat up against it.

history.text: Before this year the missionary Amand founds a church of Saint Peter at the meeting of the Leie and the Scheldt; it is an abbey before 700 and holds the grave of Bavo by the 8th century. The people threw Amand into the river more than once before they listened.
history.source: A. Verhulst, 'Ontstaan en vroegste geschiedenis van Gent' (dossier 7); nl.wikipedia Sint-Baafsabdij; en.wikipedia Saint_Amand

history.text: About this year the bones of Pharaildis (Veerle) are brought to Ganda. Her feast is the fourth of January.
In November the emperor Charles comes to the river Scheldt, to the place called Gand, and looks at the ships built there for his fleet.

On 2 June the emperor Louis takes Blandinium under his protection at the asking of its abbot, Einhard, who sets twenty-four clerics there. A later list says the house had come almost to nothing before him.
history.source: Einhard's letters and Jaffe's notes, Monumenta Carolina (1867) (dossier 5); State Archives of Belgium (dossier 9)

history.text: On 13 April Louis does the same for Saint Bavo's: the count has no power on abbey land, the abbey fines and punishes there, and owes the emperor prayers, gifts and army service. The charter survives whole, with the emperor's head in white wax; the scribe signs as Faramund.
history.source: State Archives of Belgium, the charter of 819 (dossier 9)

history.text: On 3 July relics of the martyrs Marcellinus and Peter reach Saint Bavo's. Until the end of September the sick are healed there: the blind girl Hartlinda of Furnes, the serfs Eberald and Gundrada, Liodold of Alphen on two crutches, and blind Germar from the sea-coast of the Frisians near the mouth of the Scheldt.
history.source: Einhard, Translation of Marcellinus and Peter IV.8, tr. B. Wendell (1926) (dossier 6)

history.text: Einhard is at Blandinium on 21 January and, sick, at Saint Bavo's in the spring. He came by boat from Valenciennes, and reckons fifteen days by boat from here to his house at Seligenstadt on the Main.
On 14 March Einhard dies, abbot of both houses for twenty years and more. He ruled them from Aachen.
Danes rage as far as the monastery of Saint Bavo which they call Gant, and burn it. The canons flee to Laon with Bavo's bones.
Between 858 and 865 Usuard of Paris writes 'in portu Ganda' of Saint Bavo: the first time the village on the Scheldt bank is called a port.
From about this year to 875 pennies of King Charles the Bald are struck here, reading GANDAVVM. Sixteen are known.
In November the army that had sat at Fulham on the Thames crosses the sea and takes its winter seat in the monastery of Ganda. It went 'to Ghent in Frankland, and sat there a year'.
The army wastes Tournai and the monasteries on the Scheldt, beats Abbot Gauzlin and moves to Courtrai in November. Saint Peter's on the hill is plundered that winter.
After its defeat at Saucourt the army comes back to Ganda, refits its ships and goes on to the Meuse.

Count Baldwin II dies on 10 September and is laid at last in Saint Peter's, so that his widow may one day lie by him. A charter dated the next day has her, Aelfthryth, King Alfred's daughter, give the abbey Lewisham, Greenwich and Woolwich on the Thames.
history.source: nl.wikipedia Boudewijn_II_van_Vlaanderen; Victoria County History, Kent ii, 238 (an abbey text, possibly forged (?))

history.text: On 7 June Aelfthryth dies and is buried by her husband at Saint Peter's.
By about this year the community of Saint Bavo's has come back to its burned house. Count Arnulf holds its lands.
history.source: mmmonk.be; nl.wikipedia Sint-Baafsabdij; fr.wikipedia Abbaye Saint-Bavon de Gand (dates not firm: 920 to 937)

history.text: Gerard of Brogne turns Saint Peter's from canons into monks under Benedict's Rule and is its abbot for three years; he does the same at Saint Bavo's in 946. House plots between the Scheldt and the Leie are named for the first time.
Bishop Transmar of Tournai consecrates Saint John's church inside the ditch of the port.
Dunstan, driven out of England, finds shelter at Saint Peter's for a year or more.
history.source: Victoria County History, Kent ii, 238; en.wikipedia Dunstan (about 956 to 957)

history.text: King Edgar confirms Lewisham to Saint Peter's. Count Arnulf I dies on 27 March of this year or the next.
history.source: Victoria County History, Kent ii, 238; en.wikipedia Arnulf I, Count of Flanders

history.text: The emperor Otto II takes Saint Bavo's under his protection: the Scheldt is his empire's border, and the abbey stands on the far side of it from the count.
The same year died Womare, Abbot of Ghent. Odwin becomes abbot of Saint Bavo's and begins a great stone church.
King Henry II, emperor from 1014, takes the count's castle on the Leie. In the same year the bones of a saint called Livinus are brought from Houtem to Saint Bavo's.
On 10 April the eastern pilgrim Macarius dies of the plague at Saint Bavo's. He had knocked first at Saint Peter's and been sent away.
A charter in King Edward's name confirms the Thames manors to Saint Peter's.
history.source: Victoria County History, Kent ii, 238 (an abbey text, possibly forged (?))

eras.text: King Charles's years. Two half-kept royal abbeys served by canons, a village on the Scheldt bank, sheep on the flood meadows. No market, no toll, no mint: the abbeys gather what their land yields and pass it on. Saint Peter's on the hill has few clerics and a bad roof. In 810 and 811 the bank is full of oak and the noise of adzes, and in November 811 the emperor comes to look at the ships.

Einhard's years. He is abbot of both houses from Aachen and comes seldom; his steward Erembert runs them and his letters ask for the dues in full and in good silver. Twenty-four clerics on the hill, probably the first stone church at Saint Bavo's, and from 819 a charter that keeps the count off abbey land. In the summer of 828 the sick come by boat and on crutches to the new relics.

Three kings share the realm and Ganda falls to Charles the Bald, with the Scheldt as his border. Danes hold Walcheren at the river mouth for the emperor Lothar, and the abbey's wool land there pays them. Boats still come up; fewer go down with anything worth taking.

Saint Bavo's is burned in 851 and its canons are at Laon with the saint. The village on the bank goes on without them and is called a port; for eleven years the king's pennies are struck in it. A ditch in a half circle is dug round the houses, some time in these years or after (?).

The great army from England sits in the monastery. Its ships lie along the bank, its horses on the meadows; it sells what it took in England and takes what there is in Flanders. Saint Peter's is plundered. A merchant who comes up the river comes by the army's leave.

Saint Bavo's stands roofless and empty. The counts of Flanders, Baldwin II and then Arnulf, hold the abbeys' lands and make Saint Peter's their burial church; the countess is an English king's daughter. The port inside its ditch grows slowly. Wool comes up from the sheep marshes of the coast.

Count Arnulf's years. The canons of Saint Bavo's are back; Gerard of Brogne makes monks of both houses; Saint John's is consecrated in the port, and the abbeys own every house plot in it for a yearly rent. About 950 a timber castle of the count's rises on the Leie, with a hall and grain stores. An English archbishop to be spends a winter on the hill.

A wool and cloth place now. The Scheldt is the border of the empire, and each abbey looks to a different lord across it. The two houses quarrel over which is older and write old charters to prove it. Odwin builds a great stone church at Saint Bavo's. Men of Flanders pay toll at London.

The eastern king takes the castle in 1007 and gives it back. Saints arrive: Livinus in 1007, the stranger Macarius dying in the plague of 1012. From 1038 rich families begin to buy their plots free of the abbeys' rent. English wool goes to Flemish looms (?). Saint Bavo's new church is not finished when the game ends: it is dedicated in May 1067.

sites.name: The Scheldt bank
sites.see: A long low bank of trodden clay on the left side of a wide brown river, with a dozen flat barges and small boats nosed into it and held by stakes. Downstream the thatch and one wooden tower of Saint Bavo's stand where a second river comes in; upstream, smoke from the village; behind everything, a sand hill with a church on it. Wet rope, river mud, sheep somewhere, a bell.
sites.source: Verhulst (dossier 7): boats lie on the Scheldt's left bank between the abbey and a lay village 500 m upstream; ports_793.json (riverbank). No toll is recorded in 793 (dossier 4), so there is none to pay here

sites.name: The wrights' strand
sites.see: A stretch of bank above the flood line where two hulls stand on blocks, one a flat barge nearly planked, one only a keel and ribs. Split oak is stacked under a lean-to; a pitch pot smokes on three stones; chips lie ankle deep. The sound is adzes, never saws, and a man swearing mildly at a plank.
sites.source: Annales regni Francorum 811 (ships built at Gand for the fleet); Annales Vedastini 881 (the Northmen refit their ships here); Verhulst pictures bank settlements and shipyards in the 9th century (dossier 7). Where the yard of 811 lay is not known: this place is ours

sites.name: Saint Bavo's at the meeting of the waters
sites.see: A cluster of timber and wattle buildings on the point of land between two rivers, with one larger church, limewashed, and a wooden gate where a porter sits. Inside the church a low tomb under a lamp, crutches leaning on the wall beside it. Candle smoke, wet thatch, and in a side room a chest of books with its lid propped open to air.
sites.source: Einhard, Translation I: 'the monastery of Saint Bavon, which is situated near the Scheldt in the place called Ghent, where that stream is joined with the river Lys' (Wendell 1926). The first stone church is probably Einhard's; a fort ('Gandavum castrum') is unproven (dossier 2). The librarian and the book chest: riddles_793.json (book_chest; the moth riddle)

sites.name: Saint Peter's on the hill of Blandinium
sites.see: A sand hill standing twenty metres over the flats, the only height in sight, with a church and a few houses on its top and a path worn up from the Scheldt. From the door the whole meeting of the rivers lies below: boats, both arms of the Leie, the meadows shining. At the cellar door a man is counting cheeses onto a board.
sites.source: nl.wikipedia Blandijnberg (about 29 m high); dossier 2: royal land given by Dagobert, 24 clerics under Einhard, plundered 879-80, the counts' burial church from 918, monks from 941, a vineyard on the slope at an unknown date. The Witle farm's due comes here (places/witla.json)

sites.name: The village on the bank
sites.see: Twenty or thirty thatched houses on a dry ridge along the river, each with a fenced yard, a few with a loom shed. There is no market cross and no booth: goods are shown at a house door or on an upturned boat, and the abbey's man is usually within hearing. Wool grease, peat smoke, a dog on every plot.
sites.source: Verhulst (dossier 7): a lay village on the Scheldt's left bank by the present cathedral from the early 9th century; no market, toll or fair is recorded in 793 (dossier 4). Trade here is what the abbeys and their tenants have over

sites.name: Hildrada's benches
sites.see: A long low house at the downstream end of the village, its door facing the river, with benches along the wall outside and a vat steaming in the yard. Bargemen, an abbey carter, a canon who should be elsewhere. A woman with her sleeves tied back watches the bank while she pours.
sites.source: invented; say 'ale-house'. After Hildrada's time the house is kept by her kin (the role re-forges)

sites.name: The church of the Holy Christ
sites.see: A small timber church beside the abbey fence, for the people who are not clergy: a clay floor, one glassless window, a font cut from a tree trunk. Graves crowd its south side. A grey pot with a spout, the Rhine kind, stands by the door for the holy water.
sites.source: Verhulst (dossier 7): a church beside the abbey, probably the parish church of the Holy Christ, dug at the old Beestenmarkt, the first phase perhaps timber; Carolingian layers with sherds of Rhenish Badorf ware

sites.name: The Leie meadows
sites.see: Flat wet grass cut by three or four arms of a slow river, with sheep on every dry patch and a herd's hut on stilts. In winter it is one sheet of water with fence tops showing. Larks, a sour smell of fleece, and far off the hill with its church.
sites.source: dossier 1 (sources 7, 13): the Leie runs in several arms; the meadows flood part of the year and suit sheep, not corn

sites.name: The army's winter seat
sites.see: The burned abbey with a bank and stakes thrown round it, long ships drawn up in a row below, horses picketed on the meadows as far as the eye goes. In the roofless church men sit among bales and chests and weigh silver on a folding scale. Wood smoke, horse dung, and a dozen tongues, most of them northern.
sites.source: Annales Vedastini 879: the army winters 'in Gandao monasterio'; Anglo-Saxon Chronicle 880. No dig has found the camp and nobody says who led it (dossier 8): the bank, the stakes and the market are ours

sites.name: The port inside the ditch
sites.see: House plots in rows between the Scheldt and the Leie, closed on the land side by a wet ditch in a half circle with one plank bridge. Bales of wool on the bank, cloth on rails, a man with a balance at a door. From 942 a new church of Saint John stands in the middle of it. Fulling tubs stink behind the houses.
sites.source: Usuard, 858/65: 'in portu Ganda'; the ditch found in 1987 at the Borreputsteeg, 9th-10th century, about 6 ha inside, filled in during the 10th; plots ('mansiones') named in 941, all owned by the abbeys for a yearly rent; Saint John's consecrated 942 (dossier 2). Pennies reading GANDAVVM were struck 864-75 only: changing coin here in other years is done at a merchant's door by weight

sites.name: Saint Bavo's, come back
sites.see: Old burned walls patched with new stone, monks in black where there were canons, and from the 980s a great church going up in grey Tournai stone behind a forest of poles. Masons' chips, lime, a hoist creaking. In the old church the saints lie in a row of new shrines, more of them each generation.
sites.source: dossier 2 and 5: the community returns about 920-37; monks from 946; the Romanesque church begun under Abbot Odwin (981-98) and dedicated 10 May 1067; Landoald's bones 980, Livinus 1007, Macarius 1012. Tournai stone is our guess (?)

sites.name: The count's new castle on the Leie
sites.see: A raised platform of earth and braced timber on the left bank of the Leie, with a long wooden hall, grain stores on posts and a small chapel of Saint Veerle. Below it, hides soak in pits and leather-workers scrape at beams. A keeper's man at the gate asks what is in the boat.
sites.source: The 'new castle' of the Miracles of Bavo (later 10th century); first timbers tree-ring dated no earlier than about 950; a timber-braced platform with a hall and grain stores, leather-workers beside it (disputed), a chapel of Saint Pharaildis (dossier 2). It is timber: the stone hall is after the game's end. That a toll was taken at it is ours (?)

people.name: Ansold
people.trait: The cellarer of Saint Peter's on the hill: keeps a half-empty house standing by counting everything in it twice, and asks after the cows before the people.
people.want: The dues in before Saint Bavo's Mass, wax for the altar, and the roof mended before he dies under it.
people.fear: A king's man proving that the abbey's sheep ground at the river mouth is the king's; later, an abbot who can read a tally.
people.voice: Counts aloud while he talks and loses neither thread. Never says a number he has not checked. Dry, not unkind.
people.looks: About forty-five in 793, thin, tonsured, ink and cheese-wax on his fingers, a grey wool tunic patched at the elbows, a bundle of notched tally sticks on a thong at his belt.
knows: what each of the abbey's farms owes and which has paid, from the Leie to the sea
the price of wool before shearing and after, and who on the coast will sell ahead for silver
what wax, honey and candles cost this year, and why
which boats on the bank are the abbey's and which only say so
who has the count's ear, since the count has none here that he will name

ties.note: the king's steward on Walcheren says the abbey's fold stands on the king's ground; each writes it down differently
he advanced her silver on next year's wool in the hungry spring, and has counted her fleeces carefully ever since
has never seen her: knows her by one bolt of cloth a year and five cows, and asks after the cows
her rent is paid in ale, and by his own tally the abbey has drunk a year ahead
the book-keeper at Saint Bavo's wants calfskins for leaves; the cellarer wants the calves
from 815 his abbot, who reads every tally sent to Aachen
not Ansold's own quarrel but his office's: after 841 the wool land at the river mouth pays the Dane, and the abbey writes to kings about it
the toll man down river takes his share of the abbey's boats by an old right and can show the leaf; the cellarer has asked to see it twice
one steward to another: they have exchanged tallies and never met (?)
the wright is the abbey's tenant: Ansold sets the price for mending the abbey's boats and Hildgis sets how long it takes
showed the abbot's new steward where every tally was kept, and where two were, and has regretted the second lesson
a Frisian at Mogontia sends one cask a year for the Mass, round by Dorestad, since the vines on the hill give vinegar; Ansold pays in cloth and counts the staves

lines.greet: You are the one with the small boat. Good. Small boats come when they say. Sit; I will count while we talk.
lines.greet_again: Back before Saint Bavo's Mass, and the casks not sprung. I had you down for Martinmas. I will change the tally.
rumour: Reginbert on Walcheren says our fold stands on the king's ground. The king has not said so. Until he does, the fleeces are Saint Peter's.
Witle sends one bolt and some cheeses for five cows and four people. I ask after the cows first. People can send word; cows cannot.
Honey was thin two summers running, so wax is dear. A church without candles is a barn. Bring me wax and name a fair price.
lines.saying: What is counted twice is lost once.
lines.abbot: The new abbot sits at Aachen and reads every tally. A small man. He found four pennies I had not lost yet.
lines.farewell: Go with God, and come back with the count right.

people.source: invented: the office is the Rule's and every abbey's; the id is the one places/witla.json and places/walichrum.json already use. Ans- and -old are attested Frankish name parts. The poor state of Saint Peter's before Einhard is from the 12th-century list (dossier 1). After 822 the office goes on under other men

people.name: Einold
people.trait: The canon who keeps the book chest at Saint Bavo's and fights the moth and the damp for it; teaches the boys their letters with riddles because nothing else holds them.
people.want: Calfskin, a dry room, and one more book than Saint Peter's has.
people.fear: Opening the chest after a wet winter.
people.voice: Fussy and quick; orders first, kindness after. Likes a riddle better than a sermon and is ashamed of it on feast days.
people.looks: Just past forty in 793, round-shouldered, a canon's tonsure gone ragged, a brown tunic dusted with chalk, a goose quill behind one ear and a small knife for scraping skins.
knows: every book in the two abbeys, who copied it and what it would fetch
the Latin riddles of Symphosius, and which of them a boatman can guess
the life of Bavo, who was called Allowin, and of Amand who was thrown in the river
what letters have passed through to and from the palace, because he copies the good ones
who in the district can read, which is a short list

ties.note: calves for vellum against calves for the dues: an argument now in its tenth year
has never met him; copies every letter of his that passes and calls him 'the master' (?)
the Northumbrian letter-carrier slept a night in the guest room and left the news of Lindisfarne behind him (?)
will talk to any man aboard who has Latin, and Beornwine has
they lend each other exemplars by boat and argue by the same boat about their return
her mother's brother's son; she feeds him and says so
taught him his letters at Saint Bavo's; the priest down river has a small church now and has not forgiven the difference
the list-keeper at Mogontia and he have each other's leaf-counts by way of Traiectum; Einold is sure the Rhine clerk is hiding an Aldhelm
wrote once, humbly, to ask the archbishop for the riddle Alcuin sent him about a comb, and had it by the next boat, which he had not expected (?)

lines.greet: Wipe your hands. No, on your own cloak. Now: can you read, or have you a man aboard who can?
lines.greet_again: You. Did you guess what ate the words and came away no wiser? Tell me quietly; the boys are listening.
rumour: We have eleven books and a chest. The chest is the best of them. It has never been wrong, and nothing has eaten it.
A letter from York went through here, about the heathen and Saint Cuthbert's church. I copied it before it went on. That is not theft; it is care.
Bavo sold his own people before he was a saint. Then he had one of them lead him to prison in chains. Think of it when you price one.
lines.saying: A moth reads more than a canon and is no wiser. I say nothing about the canon.
lines.riddle: Here is one for your boat. Letters fed me, and I do not know what a letter is. Come back when you have it.
lines.farewell: Go. Shut the door hard; the damp is a worse reader than the moth.

people.source: invented: he is 'the librarian of Saint Bavo's' who gives the moth riddle (riddles_793.json; texts_793.json symphosius_16_tinea: 'Littera me pavit, nec quid sit littera novi', ed. Riese 1894). In 793 the abbeys have canons, not monks (dossier 1). Ein- and -old are attested Frankish name parts. After him the office goes on

people.name: Hildgis
people.trait: The wright of the Scheldt bank: builds by eye and by his father's rods, distrusts any order that has a date in it, and has never yet launched a boat he was ashamed of.
people.want: Seasoned oak, good pitch, and a son-in-law who can hold an adze the right way up.
people.fear: Green timber, and the king's hurry.
people.voice: Grumbles in short sentences, mostly at wood. Praises nothing, so that a nod from him is worth having.
people.looks: Thirty-five in 793, broad, a short brown beard full of chips, a leather apron black with pitch, two fingers of the left hand gone at the first joint, an adze over his shoulder.
knows: what a hull needs and what it will cost, to the rivet
where oak, pitch, tar, rope and rivets come from this year and who has them
the Scheldt down to the sea and the Leie as far up as a barge floats
which boats on the bank are sound and which are for sale because they are not
what the count's man said about ships, word for word, because it worried him

ties.note: his sister; he drinks at her benches and pays, which she finds suspicious
he is the abbey's tenant and mends the abbey's boats first, at the abbey's price
a steersman who knows when a boat is tired is a wright's friend
in 810 and 811 the order for the fleet reaches him through the counts, Dorestad's among them (?)
the toll man at the landing down river counts every raft of oak that passes for Ganda, aloud, and takes his share by an old right
owes the king's steward for a raft of oak that came round by the island and was let through
the king's steward at the Ruhr mouth sells him oak from the king's forest in the two years of the emperor's order, and is the only man in that business who sent what he said

lines.greet: Mind the strake. She is not yours and she is not finished. What do you want mended, and how badly do you want it?
lines.greet_again: Your boat again. She still swims? Then I did it right or you sailed her gently. I know which I think.
rumour: The emperor wants ships by the dark end of the year. Oak wants three winters. I told the count's man. He wrote down the first part.
Pitch comes out of heathen woods and oak out of Saxon ones. The king fights one and has just done with the other. Guess what both cost.
A river barge I can build asleep. A sea ship with a keel I must be awake for, and paid as if awake.
lines.saying: Green oak and a king's hurry: both warp.
lines.emperor: He came in the dark of the year, looked at my hulls and said nothing. From an emperor, they tell me, that is praise.
lines.farewell: Keep her tarred. Come back before she opens, not after.

people.source: invented: shipwrights at Ganda are certain from the Annales regni Francorum 811 and not one is named (dossier 3). Hild- and -gis are attested Frankish name parts

people.name: Hildrada
people.trait: Brews for the bank and pays her rent to the abbey in ale; sees every boat come in and has usually guessed its business before the rope is fast.
people.want: Her son kept off the abbey's list of men owed to the host; a dry cellar.
people.fear: The Leie in a wet winter; a man counting spears.
people.voice: Says a hard thing lightly and moves on before it lands. Calls every skipper by his boat.
people.looks: Late thirties in 793, strong forearms, fair hair under a linen cloth, a russet dress with the sleeves tied back, a wooden ladle hung at her belt like a key.
knows: who is on the bank tonight, what he carries and who he is waiting for
what the canons of both houses say about each other after the third cup
when the meadows will flood, by the frogs
which bargemen can be hired and which should be
every saint's day kept here and what may not be eaten on it

ties.note: her brother, the wright; she worries about his fingers and he about her cellar
her cousin the book-keeper, whom she feeds
the abbey's tenant: her rent is ale, measured by him, never in her favour
the ale-wife of the island: smoked eels go down river, salt comes up, and with them everything either has heard
the ale-wife of the landing down river keeps a split stick for every drinker; the two send each other word of who is coming up or down
he drank here once, paid in a clipped penny and praised the ale; she has kept the penny
a potter's widow at Colonia whose grey pots reach this bank by two rivers; Hildrada asked by a bargeman who was selling to both, and had back a spouted pitcher and the answer: I am

lines.greet: Sit where I can see you. Ale is paid in silver or in news, and news is cheaper if it is true.
lines.greet_again: I kept your bench. A bargeman from up the Leie has sat on it since, but he did not improve it.
rumour: The canons say the meadows flood for our sins. They flooded before we had any. My grandmother's grandmother's sheep drowned heathen.
A barge came down from Valenciennes with grey pots, the Rhine kind, come the long way round. Somebody is selling to both rivers.
The count's man was counting spears along the bank. When they count spears, hide your sons and sell your ale.
lines.saying: Two rivers, two abbeys, one purse. Guess whose.
lines.goose: Nobody here eats goose on Saint Veerle's day. She put one back together from skin and bones. You do not want supper walking off.
lines.farewell: Mind the near arm of the Leie going out. It has a new idea every spring.

people.source: invented. -rada is as in Gundrada, a serf of Saint Bavo healed in 828 (Einhard, Translation IV.8); Hild- is attested. Pharaildis and the goose: en.wikipedia Pharaildis; that no goose is eaten on her day is invented (?). Einhard came by boat from Valenciennes in 830 (dossier 1); Badorf sherds lie under the parish church (dossier 2)

people.name: Einhard
people.trait: The emperor's friend and the old emperor's biographer, a layman set over both abbeys: small, exact, courteous, and far more often at Aachen than here.
people.want: The dues in full and in good silver; wax for his martyrs; to be left at home on the Main with his wife and his saints.
people.fear: The quarrel between the emperor and his sons, and being asked which side he is on.
people.voice: Polite and precise, with a small joke against himself in every third sentence. Asks a boatman real questions and listens to the answers.
people.looks: A very small man of about fifty in 827, neat grey beard, a good dark blue cloak pinned at the shoulder, soft riding boots, a wax tablet and stylus always in his left hand.
knows: the court: who is in favour, who is not, and what the emperor's sons are doing
what both abbeys own and what they should yield
how long the river road takes from here to the Main: he has reckoned it at fifteen days
the old emperor's wars and his ships, at first hand
the relics of Marcellinus and Peter and every cure they worked here, by name

ties.note: his master at the palace school, who made verses about how small he was (?)
his steward here, who has learned to read what a courteous letter means
taught an old cellarer that an abbot at Aachen can still count
her farm at Witle is Saint Peter's; he has never seen it and takes its bolt of cloth each year
the archbishop of Mainz (826-847), in whose province his house at Seligenstadt lies (?)
both men of the emperor Louis's court; whether they ever spoke is not recorded (?)
the archbishop of Colonia, past whose strand the wax and the letters go up to the Main; his clerks pass the abbot's packets without opening them, or reseal them well (?)

lines.greet: You came up the Scheldt? Then you have seen more of my abbeys' land than I have. Sit. Tell me what the river is doing.
lines.greet_again: The shipman. Good. I have letters and no legs for the road; the saints have made me lazy. How many days to the Main?
rumour: I reckon fifteen days by boat from here to my house on the Main. A man who does it in twelve I will remember in a letter.
Honey has failed two years. I must send a pack-load of wax home with my men after Saint Bavo's Mass, or the martyrs sit in the dark.
The old emperor stood on this bank the year the peace was sworn, counting hulls. He counted aloud. Nobody corrected him.
lines.saying: A small man sees the underside of everything: tables, horses, great men.
lines.sick: I am ill, and they want me at court. If anyone asks, you found me in bed. It has the merit of being true.
lines.farewell: Go well. If the dues come in bad silver I shall know whom not to blame; you only carry it.

people.source: Historical: abbot of Blandinium by 2 June 815 and of Saint Bavo's by 13 April 819, died 14 March 840; at Saint Bavo's in 827 and, sick, in spring 830; at Blandinium 21 January 830 (dossier 3; letters in Monumenta Carolina 1867; Translation, Wendell 1926). He did not live here: meet him only in 827 and 830. Born about 770-775. His smallness: Walahfrid's preface and Alcuin's verses (not opened (?)). The lines are ours; 'the yield of honey has been small these two years' and 'in full and in good silver' are his letters' matter (dossier 4)

people.name: Erembert
people.trait: Einhard's steward over both houses, the man who is actually here: feeds twenty-four clerics, collects from farms he has never seen, and answers letters from court.
people.want: The census gathered and sent before the letter asking for it arrives.
people.fear: A letter from Aachen that begins kindly.
people.voice: Brisk and a little hunted. Says 'the abbot writes' the way other men say 'the weather is turning'.
people.looks: About forty in 827, tall and stooped, clean-shaven, a sober green tunic with a good belt, a ring of keys and a folded letter he keeps taking out and reading again.
knows: what the abbot's last letter said and what it meant
which holders of abbey land have paid and which are waiting to see who wins at court
the price of beans, bread grain and ale in three markets
who has been healed at the relics, since he must feed the rest
which boats the abbey can lend and to whom

ties.note: his vicedominus; knows him almost wholly by letter
the old cellarer taught him where every tally was kept, and where two were
the count of Walcheren keeps the river mouth; the abbey's wool passes under his eye (?)
the abbey buys the island's salt on credit until the wool silver comes in
a palace clerk who tells him, a week ahead, what the court will want (?)

lines.greet: State your business to me. The abbot is at court and I am what there is. Is it the dues, the wax or the land?
lines.greet_again: You again, and on the day you said. I shall put that in a letter. He likes to hear that something arrived.
rumour: He writes that the dues of both houses are to be taken in full and in good silver. He underlines nothing. He does not need to.
Twenty-four clerics on the hill, where there were a handful and a leak. They all eat. I know the price of beans in three markets.
Since the relics came, every cripple on the Scheldt wants a bed. Half of them walk home. I count the other half.
lines.saying: A kind letter from court is the dearest thing a ship can bring.
lines.farewell: Go. If you meet Willibald the priest on the road with the dues, ask him how many pennies he set out with.

people.source: Historical in name and office only: Erembert the vicedominus, Liuthard the priest and Willibald the priest who collects the dues are Einhard's men in his letters (dossier 3). His years, his looks and his words are ours (?)

people.name: Ketil
people.trait: The man who sells for one ship's company of the great army: fifteen summers in England, a folding scale, and no interest in a thing once it is weighed.
people.want: Silver that is silver, and a buyer who comes twice.
people.fear: A king with ships. He met one on the Thames and has not said so.
people.voice: Says less than he means and means it flatly. Counts in ounces and marks, never in pennies.
people.looks: About forty, lean, yellow hair gone thin and tied back, a good English cloak that was made for a taller man, a silver arm ring nicked all along one edge, a folding balance in a bronze case.
knows: what the army took in England and what of it is still unsold
the weight and fineness of any silver put in front of him
where the army means to ride when the grass grows, more or less
which ships need planking and what a wright is worth to them
the Thames from Fulham to the sea

ties.note: an English seaman who trades in Danish ports is a man Ketil has bid against (?)
bought walrus rope from the Northman's people once and was not cheated, which he remembers (?)
the boy who is count of this land in name will remember whose horses stood in his abbey; Ketil has not thought about him at all
a Frisian wine carrier from the Rhine sold at the camp once in the winter of 880 and argued over the weight of every ounce; Ketil respected it and gave him nothing extra
the archbishop at the top of the Rhine shelters the priests of the towns the army burns, and in 883 rides out and takes plunder back from some of Ketil's old shipmates
the Franks' commander on the lower Rhine; the crews that go up from Ganda to the Meuse and the Rhine learn his name before they learn the rivers'

lines.greet: You came up the river with a hold and no spears. So you are a buyer or a fool. I sell to both.
lines.greet_again: The same boat. Then the last silver was good, or you would have stayed away. Sit. The ale is the abbey's.
rumour: We sat a winter at Fulham on the Thames. The English king had grown teeth. So we came where the kings are busy with each other.
There are books here with gold on the boards. The boards I can sell anywhere. The leaves only a priest wants, and priests run.
We ride up the Scheldt when the grass grows. If you have kin at Tournai, tell them it is a good year to visit elsewhere.
lines.saying: A monastery is a barn that somebody else filled.
lines.farewell: Go safely. Say at the river mouth that Ketil gave you peace. It may even help.

people.source: invented: nobody of the army at Ghent is named (Godfrid 'king of the Danes' is named with it at Thimeon, not here: dossier 3). Ketil is a common Danish name. Fulham and the crossing: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle 879-880 (Ingram 1823), which keeps this band, gathered at Fulham in 879, apart from the army King Alfred beat, which went from Cirencester to settle East Anglia. That a man with fifteen summers in England sailed with the Fulham band is invented (?). Tournai wasted: Annales Vedastini 880

people.name: Baldwin
people.trait: Baldwin II, count of Flanders, a boy when the army sat at Ganda: he has spent his life building forts against the Northmen and taking abbeys' land to pay for them.
people.want: Timber, rope and men for his forts, and every abbey between the Scheldt and the sea under his own hand.
people.fear: Another winter army; and, a little, the bishops, one of whom his man killed.
people.voice: Short and practical, a builder's talk: how much, how soon, who brings it. Does not explain himself to churchmen or merchants.
people.looks: Forty in 905, heavy in the shoulder, bald early, a short fair beard, a mail shirt under a plain green cloak, mud to the knee from walking a new ditch.
knows: every fort on the coast and the rivers, which are finished and which are only a bank
where oak, rope and pitch can be had and what he will pay, which is less than asked
what the abbeys' lands yield, since he holds them
the English court, through his wife
where the Northmen on the Seine are this year

ties.note: his wife, King Alfred's daughter; he will be moved in his coffin so that she can lie beside him
the count buys up the oak the carpenter across the river wants (?)
the Northman on the Seine is the neighbour his forts face
he was about fourteen when the army took Ganda; he has not forgotten whose abbey they stabled in

lines.greet: A shipman. Good. What do you carry, where from, and can you bring oak? Answer the last one first.
lines.greet_again: You brought what you said. Most do not. Next time bring rope as well; I will pay at the bank, in pennies.
rumour: They sat in that abbey a year when I was a boy. Now there is a ditch and a bank at every river mouth. Let them come and count.
The monks say I hold their land. I hold it between them and the sea. They may have it back when the sea is quiet.
My wife's father built ships and burhs and had it all written down. I build, and let the monks write what they like.
lines.saying: A bank and a ditch pray all night and ask no tithe.
lines.farewell: Go. If you see sails at the river mouth, tell the first man with a spear, not the first with a tonsure.

people.source: Historical: Baldwin II, count 879-918, died 10 September 918, buried at Saint Peter's; husband of Aelfthryth; fort-builder against the Northmen (realms/francia.md: 'Flanders builds forts'); the counts held the abbeys' lands (dossier 3, 5). Born about 865 (?). His man killed Archbishop Fulk of Reims in 900 (not in the dossier (?)). Whether the castle at Ganda is his is disputed: the timbers say about 950, so he is met on the hill, not in a castle. His words are ours. places/andoverpis.json also uses this id for Baldwin IV (988-1035), who took the same name and the same quarrels: see ganda.baldwin_v

people.name: Baldwin
people.trait: Baldwin V, count of Flanders: the French king's brother-in-law, the Norman duke's father-in-law, and host to every English exile of his time. He keeps all of them, and tells none what he thinks.
people.want: The right bank of the Scheldt, and to be owed something by whoever wins in England.
people.fear: The emperor on the river again, as in his father's day.
people.voice: Easy and unhurried; asks after your trade as though it were his own, and remembers the answer a year later.
people.looks: About forty in 1051, tall, greying brown hair cut round, a long tunic of good Flemish blue with a fur collar, a seal ring he turns while he listens.
knows: who is in exile from England this year and at whose table he sits
what the Norman duke is building, since the duke's wife is his daughter
the tolls of London as they fall on the men of Flanders
the price of English wool and of Flemish cloth, better than a count should
the march across the river and how many men hold it

ties.note: the margrave across the Scheldt was set there to deny Flanders the right bank, to this count and to his father Baldwin IV before him
in 1055 his men burn every house outside the wall across the river, hers among them (?)
Cnut's widow Emma wintered in Flanders under his protection in 1037 (?)
the English earl, driven out in 1051, winters under his roof and sails home from his coast the next summer (?)
the duke of the Normans is his daughter Matilda's husband from about 1051

lines.greet: Sit down. You have come from the Thames or the Seine; I can smell which. Tell me what wool is fetching.
lines.greet_again: The house with the long memory. Your father sat in that chair, or one like it. What are they saying at London?
rumour: There is always an Englishman at my table who was an earl last year. I feed them all. One of them will be owed to.
My daughter's husband builds ships along the whole coast of Normandy. He has not told me why. He has not needed to.
The emperor's margrave sits across the river to watch me. I watch him back. It costs us both a great deal of oak.
lines.saying: Keep every exile. Kings are made of them.
lines.farewell: Go safely. Come back at midwinter and tell me who sits where in England. I like to hear it from somebody who was there.

people.source: Historical: Baldwin V, count 1035-1067, born about 1012; his daughter Matilda married William of Normandy about 1051; he sheltered Queen Emma (1037), Earl Godwin (1051) and Tostig (1065) (not in the dossier: general knowledge (?)). His father Baldwin IV (988-1035), buried at Saint Peter's, lost the castle to Henry II in 1007 (dossier 3, 5). The feud with the march of Antwerp is places/andoverpis.json's. His seat was more often Bruges or Lille: meet him here on a feast. His words are ours

people.name: Aelfthryth
people.trait: King Alfred's daughter, wife and then widow of Count Baldwin II: lettered, exact about news, twenty years and more in Flanders and still asking the price of bread in Wessex.
people.want: True word from England, and to lie beside her husband on the hill.
people.fear: Her sons Arnulf and Adelolf dividing what their father held.
people.voice: Asks questions in order and expects answers in order. Dry; kind to people who do not flatter her.
people.looks: Forty in 918, straight-backed, a widow's white linen veil over a dark red gown, a small gold cross on a cord, an English psalter carried by a girl behind her.
knows: the English court as her kin's letters tell it, a season late
what the count's sons hold and which of the count's men serves which
the abbey of Saint Peter's, its lands and its dead
the Thames below London, where her own land lies
what her father had seamen tell him of the north, as a child hears such things

ties.note: her husband, the count; she has him brought from Saint-Bertin to Saint Peter's so that she can lie beside him
her father had the Northman's voyage written down; she heard it told as a girl (?)
the same, of the seaman who sailed to Truso (?)
her husband killed an archbishop and feared no man but the Northmen on the Seine; she has not forgotten which neighbour is which (?)
London is her brother's and then her nephew's; its reeve is her kin's man and knows her name
a carpenter across the Scheldt who wants the same oak her husband's forts want; she has heard his name only as a price

lines.greet: You have been in England this year? Then sit. Which river, which reeve, and what did bread cost? Leave nothing out to be polite.
lines.greet_again: The shipman who answers what is asked. Good. Is London still my kin's, and do they still ask your business twice?
rumour: My father had seamen tell him their voyages and wrote them down. Tell me yours plainly. I was brought up on better liars than you.
My lord lies on the hill at Saint Peter's. They brought him from Saint-Bertin, where no woman may lie. I mean to be beside him.
I have given Saint Peter's my land at Lewisham on the Thames. They will need a ship that knows that river. Ships can be asked.
lines.saying: A king's daughter is a letter sent abroad. One hopes it is read.
lines.farewell: God keep you on the water. Greet the Thames for me. It will not answer, but greet it.

people.source: Historical: daughter of King Alfred, married Baldwin II between 893 and 899, widowed 10 September 918, died 7 June 929, buried at Saint Peter's (dossier 3; en.wikipedia Aelfthryth, Countess of Flanders). Born about 877 (?). Baldwin was moved from Saint-Bertin so she could lie by him. The Lewisham grant of 11 September 918 is an abbey text, possibly forged (VCH Kent ii, 238) (?): she speaks of it here as the abbey's own tradition has it. There is no role for a countess, so she stands as 'widow'; before 918 she is the count's wife. Her words are ours

stories.title: Ships by the dark end of the year
stories.summary: In 810 two hundred Danish ships strip the Frisian islands, and the emperor orders a fleet built on his rivers. At Ganda the order lands on Hildgis the wright, who has the hands for it and neither the oak, the pitch nor the rivets; in November 811 the emperor himself comes to look at what was done.
stories.picture: A river bank in thin November light: a row of new hulls on blocks, pale and unpainted, wrights standing with their caps off, and a very tall old man in a plain fur cloak walking slowly along the keels with a small crowd keeping two paces behind him.

beats.text: A count's man reads the order on the bank: sea ships, by the end of next year. Hildgis says oak wants three winters and is told the emperor has not got three winters. He needs oak, pitch, tar, rope and rivets, and will pay over the common price for any brought before the frost.

Saxon oak comes down the Hellweg to the Rhine now that the Saxon war is done, and Raginhard the steward sells the king's own trunks from the forest behind the hill. A load of ten planks is thirty pennies here and half as much again at Ganda this year; every yard on the rivers is asking.

Rivets and boat nails are a Colonia trade. Bero and every smith in the row are hammering them by the keg for the emperor's hulls, and for once the clerk Hrotbert walks down the row and finds exactly what he was told he would.

Every raft of oak and every keg of rivets bound for Ganda passes the toll post at Andoverpis. Adalwin counts them aloud and takes his tenth by an old right; told that it is the emperor's timber, he says the toll is older than the emperor.

Pitch and tar are northern goods, and the north is the enemy. What reaches Dorestad came through Frisian hands before the fleet did. Ravn looks at the barrels and says he knows whose woods they are from, and no more.
The abbey's list of men owed to the host has been read out, and Hildrada's son is on it. A wright's hand is excused. Hildgis could take the boy on, if he had the timber to keep another man busy.
The emperor comes to the Scheldt, to the place called Gand, and looks at the ships. He walks the whole row. If your timber is in them, Hildgis tells the count's man so, loudly, in front of everybody.

endings.how: Brought oak, pitch and rivets in time and at a price Hildgis could pay.
endings.text: The ships are ready when the emperor comes, and the wright says whose boat carried the timber. A clerk writes the name down. Hildrada's son is kept at the yard and off the host's list.
endings.reward: Standing with the king's men in Flanders and the delta (deed kept_commission); Hildgis a fast friend, who builds and mends for this house at cost; the guard-ship unlock at Ganda opens sooner; Hildrada's bench and her news for life.

endings.how: Brought the goods and held out for the highest price the hurry would bear.
endings.text: The hulls are finished and the yard is poorer for it. Hildgis pays, counts the rivets twice, and afterwards mends your boat exactly as well as you paid him to.
endings.reward: Silver: half as much again as a good voyage, once; Hildgis cool; the cellarer notes it, without comment, on a tally.

endings.how: Let Ravn's friends know how many hulls stood on the bank and how far along they were.
endings.text: Nothing comes of it: the Danish king is dead by his own man's hand and peace is sworn on the Eider before a single hull is wet. But Ravn knows what you were willing to do, and so do you.
endings.reward: A friend's welcome at Sliesthorp for some years; Ravn says more than he did; if it is ever known in Francia, the king's men remember (deed bribed_officer turned about: standing lost with the Franks).

endings.text: The ships are built anyway, of green oak, and two open their seams in the first winter. Hildgis says he told them. The emperor comes, looks and goes back to Aachen.
endings.reward: Nothing lost. Hildgis's line about the emperor, and a yard that has learned to build sea ships.

stories.reward: A wright who builds for the house at cost and a name written down by a royal clerk, or one very good sale, or a debt of silence with Ravn.

stories.title: Wool before the shearing
stories.summary: In the hungry spring the cellarer of Saint Peter's sends silver down river to buy next year's wool from the marsh farmers while they have no bread, and wants a small quiet boat to carry it. On Walcheren the king's steward says the sheep stand on the king's ground, and the woman who took the silver has eaten it.
stories.picture: A salt marsh under a wide sky: a woman in a grey cloak counting fleeces onto the mud beside a small boat, a thin cleric with tally sticks counting them again, and on the dune behind them a man on a horse watching both.

beats.text: Ansold counts sixty pennies into a bag and ties it with his own knot. It is for Bernhild on the island, against her wool at the shearing: a price fixed now, in a spring when silver buys bread and wool buys nothing. He asks you to carry it and to say what you see.

Bernhild takes the bag, weighs it in her hand and says the abbey's man has never once counted short in her favour. She has sixty ewes, a sick sister and no rye. She asks what a sack of rye costs up river, and whether you have one.

Reginbert the king's steward has heard about the silver. The fold, he says, is on the king's ground, so the wool is the king's to sell and the abbey has bought air. He would like it said before a witness, by somebody who carried the bag.
At Saint Peter's farm on the Maas mouth the due is one bolt and some cheeses for five cows and four people, hunger or no. Thiadlint asks if you are going to Ganda anyway.

Coming up with the fleeces you pass the toll post at Andoverpis. Adalwin counts the abbey's wool like anybody's and takes his share by an old right; the cellarer's blessing, sent ahead by a bargeman, he hangs on the post with the others.
After the shearing Ansold counts the fleeces off your boat, twice, and asks whether the cows at Witle are alive. Then he asks, more carefully, what Reginbert said and who heard him say it.

endings.how: Carried the silver down and the full count of wool back, and said nothing before Reginbert's witness.
endings.text: The abbey has its wool at the spring price and a boat it trusts. Ansold writes a line under Saint Peter's seal: this man carries for us. Reginbert writes something too, elsewhere.
endings.reward: A yearly carrying commission for Saint Peter's (wool up, silver and wax down); lodging on the hill; the first step toward the abbey's own river ship; Reginbert cool.

endings.how: Sold or gave Bernhild rye at the king's price and brought the abbey a short count, saying why.
endings.text: Ansold hears you out, counts the fleeces a third time and takes the loss onto a tally of its own. He does not thank you. At Martinmas a cheese comes up river with no word attached.
endings.reward: Bernhild a fast friend and her cheese first to you each year; the thread's flag hy_fed_poor; alms reckoned to you (deed gave_alms); Ansold cool for a season, then easy: he respects a true count.

endings.how: Stood witness for Reginbert that the abbey bought wool on the king's ground.
endings.text: The steward has his witness and the abbey has a lawsuit that will outlive everybody in it. The wool is seized for the king. Bernhild keeps the silver, since nobody can agree whose it was.
endings.reward: Standing with the king's men; Reginbert friendly and his word for you at Noviomagus; Ansold wary, and no abbey commission while he lives.

stories.reward: The abbey's carrying trade, or a friend on the marsh who feeds you first, or the king's steward's good word: not all three.

stories.title: Fifteen days to the Main
stories.summary: In the summer of 828 the relics of two Roman martyrs lie at Saint Bavo's and the sick of the whole Scheldt come to them. Their keeper, the small courteous abbot Einhard, needs wax, letters and a book carried to his house on the Main, which he reckons at fifteen days by boat, and would like to know if a merchant can count better than he can.
stories.picture: The inside of a timber church at night, crowded: a low tomb under a blaze of candles, crutches stacked against the wall, a blind man being led forward by a boy, and at the side a very small man in a blue cloak writing names on a wax tablet.

beats.text: The relics came on the third of July. A blind girl from Furnes sees; two serfs of the house are healed; a man from Alphen leaves two crutches on the wall. Erembert is feeding all of them and writing every name down for the abbot.
A blind man called Germar, from the Frisian shore by the river mouth, has heard of the saints at Ganda and has no boat and no one to lead him. He can pay nothing. He knows the tides by ear.

Einhard asks how many days you make it to the Main. Honey has failed two years; he wants a pack-load of wax taken to his house at Seligenstadt after Saint Bavo's Mass, with letters, and a book brought back that he lent and has not seen again.
The boats of the sick lie a tide at the werf at Andoverpis on their way up to the relics. The ale-wife's granddaughter counts crutches coming up the river and, by Michaelmas, fewer going down.

At Colonia Archbishop Hadebald's clerks pass the abbot's wax and letters through without toll. The bishop asks whether Einhard still has a psalter of Saint Peter's, lent five years ago, and whether a boat going back might carry it.

Past Colonia and up to Mogontia, where Archbishop Otgar lodges the abbot's men, then into the Main. The wax is counted at the abbot's house by a priest who expected you a week later, and the lent book is found under another man's bed.

Einhard lies sick at Saint Bavo's while the emperor's sons rise against their father, and the court wants him. He reads the letters you bring twice and asks you to tell anyone who asks that you found him in bed.

endings.how: Carried the wax and the letters to the Main in fewer than fifteen days and brought the book back whole.
endings.text: The martyrs have their candles. Einhard corrects his reckoning on the tablet and writes a letter in which a shipman is named, which will be read at Aachen by men who buy things.
endings.reward: Einhard a fast friend; a letter of his that opens doors at the palace and at Colonia and Mogontia (standing in the Rhineland); the book trade's flag bk_carried; a good freight paid in good silver.

endings.how: Took Germar up river from the Scheldt mouth for nothing and led him to the tomb.
endings.text: He sees, or says he does, and afterwards steers your boat down to the sea by ear as he always could. Einhard writes his name in the book of the miracles, and yours is not in it; Germar's kin on the coast know whose boat it was.
endings.reward: Alms reckoned to you (deed gave_alms); a pilot for the Scheldt mouth who asks no fee while he lives; welcome on the Frisian shore of the delta; Erembert easy.

endings.how: Took the freight and came to the Main after the feast, or with the wax short.
endings.text: The house on the Main had bought candles at the dear price by then. Einhard is courteous about it in a letter that Erembert reads to you slowly.
endings.reward: The freight money, less the shortfall; no letter; Erembert pays abbey carriage on arrival only, from then on.

stories.reward: A courtier's letter and a road up the Rhine, or a pilot and the coast's good word: and either way the fifteen days, which the house may reckon by afterwards.

stories.title: Sat there a year
stories.summary: In November 879 the army that had gathered at Fulham on the Thames crosses the sea and takes the burned abbey for its winter seat. It has the takings of England in its ships, books, plate and people, and it sells; and when it comes back from its beating at Saucourt it wants wrights for its hulls.
stories.picture: A roofless church in snow, fires burning on its floor: bales and chests stacked where the altar was, a lean fair man weighing a gilt book cover on a small balance, and through the broken west door a row of long ships drawn up on a white bank.

beats.text: At the landing down river they say it plainly: stay off the Scheldt. People from the farms above are sleeping in the church. A priest asks any boat going up, in God's name, to look for what was taken from his altar.

Ketil gives a merchant peace for the length of a bargain. He has gospel books in jewelled boards, chalices, English pennies by the bag, and a clerk from a Thames minster who can write. The boards he will sell apart from the leaves, if nobody stops him.

On the Rhine they hear of the army at Ganda as of weather on another river. In the ale-house in the tower at Colonia a skipper who sold there says the Danes paid in English pennies and asked how far up the Rhine a keel can go. He was not asked twice what he answered.
What the army did not sell at Ganda it carries to the Meuse and the Rhine. In the winter of 883 a Frisian at Diusburg is offered, from the fort, a gilt book cover he last saw on Ketil's balance.
A priest on the Strand can name the book by its first words and the clerk by his mother. The minster has little silver left, and offers what it has, and prayers.
A man of the port of Ganda, carried off by the Northmen, is at Rouen and not free. He says Saint Bavo will bring him home. He would take a boat.

The army is back from Saucourt with fewer men and the same ships, and the ships need planks. The old wright's grandson is offered silver by weight to refit them. He asks you what you would do, and whether you have oak.

endings.how: Bought the book whole and the clerk with it, and carried both home to the Thames.
endings.text: The minster rings what bells it has. The clerk writes your name in the margin of the book he was sold with. It cost more than it paid, in silver.
endings.reward: Standing with the English and with every church on both shores (deed bought_captives, as a ransom; deed gave_alms); the book road's worth learned; a friend in a London minster for the heir; Ketil thinks you a fool and trades with you again.

endings.how: Bought the army's plate and pennies by weight and sold them where nobody asked.
endings.text: It is the best winter's trade the house has had. At Ganda afterwards the people who came back to the bank know which boat lay at the army's camp, and so does the bishop of Tournai.
endings.reward: Silver: two good voyages' worth; the thread's flag en_followed_silver; standing lost with Frankish churchmen for a generation; Ketil friendly, and his word good with other Danes at sea.

endings.how: Found the man of the port at Rouen and brought him home.
endings.text: He walks up the bank at Ganda carrying nothing and goes straight to the burned church. Later the monks will write it down as the saint's miracle. He names his first son after your steersman.
endings.reward: A household in the port that is yours to lodge and store with for two generations; a plot there offered to the house first when plots are named (941); standing in Flanders.

endings.how: Sold the army oak and found it hands for the refit.
endings.text: The ships go to the Meuse sound and dry, and burn Liege, Maastricht and Tongeren from them. The silver was honest weight.
endings.reward: Silver by weight, well paid; a Norse ship offered second-hand at the price of her timber; Franks from the Scheldt to the Meuse shun the house's name for years.

stories.reward: A book and a man brought home, or a hold of loot silver, or a household that owes the house its father: each remembered by different people.

stories.title: The land on the Thames
stories.summary: Saint Peter's holds Lewisham, Greenwich and Woolwich on the Thames by the gift, it says, of a count's widow who was an English king's daughter. For a century and a half the abbey needs a boat that knows that river to bring its rents home, a different English king to say the land is still its own, and nobody to look too closely at the ink.
stories.picture: A monk and a merchant bent over a charter on a table by a window, the monk's finger on a line of it; through the window, far below the hill, a small ship lying on a wide brown river.

beats.text: The countess Aelfthryth, a widow since the tenth of September, says she has given Saint Peter's her land at Lewisham for her lord's soul and her sons'. She wants a ship that knows the Thames to take the abbey's man over and see what the land yields.
Lewisham lies on a creek below London. The reeve there has never heard of an abbey in Flanders and would like to see something written. What the abbey's man shows him is very clean.

An English abbot, driven out by his young king, is wintering on the hill: Dunstan, who was at Glastonbury. He has never seen monks keep the Rule as these do. He asks every English-going boat for news, and gives letters to the ones he trusts.

At Billingsgate the toll rules are read out to every keel, and the men of Flanders are named in them. In 1012 the army lies at Greenwich, on the abbey's own land, and kills the archbishop there. No rent comes home that year.

The men of Colonia sail to the Thames in their own ships now and are read out at Billingsgate as the emperor's men, in the same list as the men of Flanders. A Colonia wine house offers to carry the abbey's rents home cheaper than a Flemish keel, and Saint Peter's cellarer wants to know what your house will say to that.

The abbey has a new charter in King Edward's name and an old story that he vowed these lands at Ganda as an exile. A monk copies the countess's grant afresh, since the old leaf, he says, was hard to read.

endings.how: Carried the abbey's man and its rents between the Thames and the Scheldt, year on year, and asked nothing about the ink.
endings.text: The house becomes Saint Peter's ship for England. Three kings confirm the land and each time a merchant of the house stands at the back of the hall.
endings.reward: A yearly commission between Ganda and Lundenwic that passes to the heir; the abbey's line read at Billingsgate (a lower toll for a man of Flanders); lodging on the hill; under Cnut, the flag en_cnut_peace is easier won.

endings.how: Carried the exile's letters to England in 956 and 957 and brought the answers.
endings.text: The young king dies, the exile goes home and is archbishop within three years. He does not forget the hill, or the boat.
endings.reward: A friend at Canterbury for a generation (deed carried_letters); the house's name in the book of life at Saint Peter's; an English charter of passage worth more than the freight.

endings.how: Told the reeve at London what the cellar door hears: that the leaf is newer than the gift.
endings.text: The reeve thanks you and does nothing, since the king has already confirmed it. The abbey learns who said so. Its rents cross in another man's boat.
endings.reward: The reeve's trust at London (he asks your word on other men's charters, for a fee); Saint Peter's shut to the house; Saint Bavo's, which is glad of anything against the hill, opens its door instead.

stories.reward: The abbey's English carrying for the house's heirs, or an archbishop's friendship, or a London reeve who takes your word: and a lesson in what a charter is.

works.name: A corner of Saint Peter's cellar
works.what: Room in the abbey's cellar on the hill for a few casks and bales, under the cellarer's tally. It is dry, it is counted, and it is a steep carry from the bank.
works.needs: The cellarer at least easy with you.
works.gives: Store up to a boatload at Ganda. Goods stored here are lost if they are still on the hill in the winter of 879.
works.picture: A low cellar with a clay floor: abbey casks in a row, and at the end three smaller ones chalked with a different mark, a tally stick hung above them.
works.source: works_793.json store_corner; Saint Peter's plundered in the winter of 879-80 (dossier 2)

works.name: Sheep on the Leie meadows
works.what: A share of ewes run with the abbey's flock on the flood meadows, shorn with it and counted with it. The wool is yours; the lambs are halved; in a wet winter some drown.
works.needs: A commission kept for either abbey.
works.gives: A few sacks of raw wool each year at shearing, before Saint John's day, at no price but the herd's share; fewer after a flood winter.
works.picture: Sheep on a green flat between two river arms, one in ten with a red daub on its rump, a herd leaning on a pole beside a hut on stilts.
works.source: works_793.json flock_share; dossier 1 and 4: the meadows suit sheep, and from about 950 the abbeys' wool is the place's trade

works.name: A slip and a shed on the wrights' strand
works.what: A plank slip above the flood line and a thatched shed over it, beside the wright's own, on ground held of the abbey for a yearly rent in pennies.
works.needs: The wright friendly, or the story of the emperor's ships ended in his favour.
works.gives: Repair and careening at Ganda cost less and take fewer days; a boat may winter here under cover; a second hull may be kept.
works.picture: A small open-sided shed on a river bank with a clinker boat hauled up under it on rollers, snow on the thatch, a wright's larger shed beside it.
works.source: works_793.json boat_shed; all ground here is the abbeys', held for rent (dossier 4)

works.name: The house's names in Saint Bavo's book
works.what: The names of the house's dead and living written in the book that lies on the altar at Mass, so that they are prayed for with the abbey's own.
works.needs: A gift large enough to be remembered; not in the years 851 to 936, when the house stands empty.
works.gives: Standing with churchmen along the Scheldt; the heir is known at Saint Bavo's on his first visit; a place to remember the dead.
works.picture: An open book on an altar cloth, two columns of names in brown ink, a canon's finger resting under the last and newest line.
works.source: works_793.json book_of_life; unlocks_793.json memorial_book_of_life (Ganda is listed)

works.name: A plot in the port, held of the abbey
works.what: A house plot between the Scheldt and the Leie, inside the ditch. The ground stays the abbey's and a rent is owed for it every year; from 1038 a rich house can buy the rent off for good.
works.needs: Standing in Flanders; a man of the port to speak for you.
works.gives: A door of your own to sell from at Ganda, a loom shed if you build one, lodging without a host; after 1038, for a further payment, the plot free of rent and heritable.
works.picture: A narrow fenced plot running from a muddy lane down to the river, a timber house at the lane end, wool bales under the eaves, a ditch and a plank bridge beyond.
works.source: works_793.json plot; plots ('mansiones') named in 941, all owned by the abbeys for a yearly rent, bought off by rich families 1038-1120 (dossier 4)

works.name: A pier of Saint Bavo's new church
works.what: Stone, lime and masons' wages for one pier of the great church the abbots are raising over the burned one. It is a long work: begun in the 980s, it is not dedicated until 1067.
works.needs: A gift carried to the abbot in person; stone brought up the Scheldt counts toward the cost.
works.gives: High standing with the abbey and the empire's side of the river; the house's mark cut on the pier; burial for the house's dead in the abbey ground.
works.picture: A half-built stone nave open to the sky, wooden scaffolding round a single finished pier, a mason cutting a small mark into its base while a monk looks on.
works.source: works_793.json church_rebuilt; the Romanesque church begun under Abbot Odwin (981-98), dedicated 10 May 1067 (dossier 2)

ships.how: built to order over a winter
ships.note: The bank's own work: flat barges for the Scheldt and the Leie, towed up against the stream. The abbeys' wool and corn move in them.
ships.picture: A long flat barge on blocks, nearly planked, pale new oak against a grey river.
ships.source: ship_classes_793.json river_barge; Einhard came by boat from Valenciennes in 830 (dossier 1)

ships.note: Every house on the Leie arms has a punt for the meadows and the crossing between the two abbeys. One can always be had.
ships.picture: A flat punt tied to a willow stump in flooded grass, a single pole laid across her.
ships.source: ship_classes_793.json skiff_punt; the Leie runs in several arms (dossier 1)

ships.note: River freighters on a log keel come down the Scheldt from Tournai and Valenciennes and are sometimes sold here rather than hauled home.
ships.picture: A round-bottomed river freighter nosed into a clay bank, empty, her crew sitting on the gunwale with their feet in the water.
ships.source: ship_classes_793.json logboat_expanded (?): no hull has been found at Ghent

ships.how: built to order over a winter
ships.note: After the emperor's order the yard knows how to lay a keel for the sea. From then a sea-going merchant ship can be ordered here, if the buyer brings the oak or the price of it.
ships.picture: A deep round-hulled ship with a single mast stepped, standing on a slip above a river, two wrights caulking her seams with tarred wool.
ships.source: ship_classes_793.json north_sea_merchant_ship; Annales regni Francorum 811 (ships built at Gand). That the skill stayed is ours (?)

ships.note: The abbeys' own river ship, lent, never sold: a merchant who has kept three commissions may be asked to master her for a season and load beside the abbey's goods.
ships.picture: A long river boat with a low wooden cabin amidships, eight oars shipped, a cleric in a dark cloak stepping aboard from a plank.
ships.source: ship_classes_793.json river_estate_ship; story/ships_793.json built_at (Ganda); unlocks_793.json unlock_ship_river_estate_ship

ships.note: The emperor's fleet ships, built here in 810 and 811. They are never a merchant's own: a trusted man may serve a season in one, or sell to her.
ships.picture: A long low rowing ship, new and unpainted, lying at a river bank with thirty oars stacked beside her and no crew yet.
ships.source: ship_classes_793.json warship_west; Annales regni Francorum 811; unlocks_793.json (the guard ship, Ganda listed)

ships.note: When the army refits after Saucourt it leaves behind hulls it has no crews for. One can be bought for the price of her timber by a man whom nobody will thank for buying.
ships.picture: A lean clinker ship with a carved stem, lying on her side on a trampled bank, three strakes stove in, a burned abbey behind her.
ships.source: ship_classes_793.json norse_allround_ship; Annales Vedastini 881 (the Northmen refit their ships at Ghent). The hull left behind is ours

sayings.text: They threw the first priest in the river. He came out and baptised them in it.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner, from the Life of Amand: the people of Ganda threw him in the river more than once (dossier 6)

sayings.text: The yield of honey has been small these two years.
sayings.source: Einhard, letters (Monumenta Carolina 1867), Englished in the dossier: his reason for sending a pack-load of wax after the Mass of Saint Bavo. Said here of anything that is short

sayings.text: In full and in good silver.
sayings.source: Einhard's order for the census of both abbeys (letters, Monumenta Carolina 1867; dossier 4). The steward's whole creed

sayings.text: Letters fed me, and I do not know what a letter is. I lived in books and am no more learned for it.
sayings.source: Symphosius, riddle 16, the moth (texts_793.json symphosius_16_tinea; Latin ed. Riese 1894); the plain English is ours. The book-keeper says it of his pupils

sayings.text: They went to Ghent in Frankland, and sat there a year.
sayings.source: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle 880 (Ingram 1823). After 881 it is said of any guest who will not leave

sayings.text: Saint Peter's kept the door shut and Saint Bavo's got the saint.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner, after 1012: Macarius knocked first at Saint Peter's and was sent away (dossier 7)

sayings.text: He lived in a hollow tree, and the abbey has been short of room ever since.
sayings.source: a canon's joke, invented; Bavo's hollow tree is from his Life (dossier 7)

sayings.text: Do not count a goose eaten at Ganda.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner: Pharaildis brought a cooked goose back to life from skin and bones (dossier 7)

sayings.text: Two abbeys, and each the elder.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner, from about 950, when the two houses fought over which was older and forged charters to prove it (dossier 6)

easter_eggs.text: Ask to see the emperor's charter at Saint Bavo's after 819: a whole skin, with Louis's head pressed in white wax at the foot, and the scribe's name where a careful reader finds it, Faramund. It is still whole twelve hundred years on.
easter_eggs.source: State Archives of Belgium, the charter of 13 April 819 (dossier 7, 9)

easter_eggs.text: In 830 Erembert is tying a bundle of the abbot's letters between boards for the chest. After the fire of 851 a canon carries that bundle to Laon under his arm. It is the only copy there will ever be.
easter_eggs.source: Einhard's letters survive in one 9th-century book, thought to have gone to Laon with the fleeing canons and found there in 1636 (dossier 7)

easter_eggs.text: The holy-water pot by the door of the Holy Christ church is grey Rhine ware with a spout. Nobody remembers who brought it. Its sherds will be found under the floor.
easter_eggs.source: Carolingian layers with sherds of Rhenish Badorf ware under the church at the old Beestenmarkt (Verhulst; dossier 2)

easter_eggs.text: Two crutches hang on the wall by Bavo's tomb from the summer of 828, shorter than most. The porter says a man from Alphen walked home without them.
easter_eggs.source: Einhard, Translation IV.8 (Wendell 1926): Liodold of Alphen, on two crutches

easter_eggs.text: An old ferryman on the Scheldt will tell you that a holy girl once crossed here standing on a sturgeon. He points to where. He has never caught one that size.
easter_eggs.source: Amalberga of Temse and the sturgeon: en.wikipedia Amalberga of Temse (dossier 7)

easter_eggs.text: After 1007 a monk shows the shrine of Saint Livinus, an Irish bishop martyred near by. A merchant who has been to Daventre may think the story sounds like Lebuin's, and keep it to himself.
easter_eggs.source: Livinus is thought to be invented, copied from Lebuin of Deventer; in 1984 Landoald's shrine held a forged 11th-century bishop's seal (dossier 7)

easter_eggs.text: In 951 the keeper's wife at the new castle has a son, baptised Arnulf. He will be count of the Frisians and die fighting them.
easter_eggs.source: Arnulf of Holland, born at Ghent in 951, son of the castle-keeper Dirk II (dossier 3; dates not firm (?))

easter_eggs.text: On the south slope of the hill a few rows of vines are tied to stakes, facing the Scheldt. The wine is the Mass's, and thin.
easter_eggs.source: a vineyard on the slope of Blandinium toward the Scheldt, date unknown (nl.wikipedia Sint-Pietersabdij (Gent)) (?)

easter_eggs.text: Between 864 and 875 a penny from the port reads GANDAVVM round the king's monogram. Keep one: sixteen are all that will be left.
easter_eggs.source: deniers of Charles the Bald reading GANDAVVM (Verhulst); sixteen known (numista, search summary only (?))

unlocks.how: Visit the book-keeper at Saint Bavo's with Latin aboard: a reader, a monk to read it out, or lessons taken.
unlocks.gives: give_text symphosius_16_tinea; answering it makes Einold friendly, and he lends a book to copy.

unlocks.what: Saint Peter's own carrier on the Scheldt
unlocks.how: End 'Wool before the shearing' with the full count, or carry the Witle due (places/witla.json, witla.saint_peters_carrier) and bring news of the cows.
unlocks.gives: commission: wool up river and silver or wax down, each year; act:lodge and act:store on the hill at no cost.

unlocks.what: Hildgis builds and mends for the house at cost
unlocks.how: End 'Ships by the dark end of the year' with your timber in the hulls.
unlocks.gives: Repair, careening and building at Ganda at the wright's own cost, for this house and its heir; the north_sea_merchant_ship may be ordered here from 811.

unlocks.what: The abbey's river ship for a season
unlocks.how: Keep three commissions for either abbey (deed kept_commission, three times).
unlocks.gives: Ship class river_estate_ship, lent (unlocks_793.json unlock_ship_river_estate_ship): the abbey's goods go free wherever its charter runs, and yours ride beside them.

unlocks.what: A letter of Einhard's that names you
unlocks.how: End 'Fifteen days to the Main' in under fifteen days.
unlocks.gives: Standing in the Rhineland and at the palace; act:audience is not refused at Colonia, Mogontia or Noviomagus while he lives (to 840); the flag bk_carried.

unlocks.what: A blind pilot for the Scheldt mouth
unlocks.how: End 'Fifteen days to the Main' by bringing Germar to the relics.
unlocks.gives: hire_pilot between Walichrum and Ganda costs nothing and is never refused, until about 845.

unlocks.how: End 'The land on the Thames' as the abbey's ship.
unlocks.gives: A yearly commission between Ganda and Lundenwic, inherited; a lower toll at Billingsgate as a man of Flanders (from about 1000).

unlocks.what: A household in the port that owes the house a father
unlocks.how: End 'Sat there a year' by bringing the man of the port home from Rouen.
unlocks.gives: act:lodge and act:store in the port at no cost for two generations; the work 'A plot in the port' at half its price from 941.

The editor's pass of 7 October 2026. The army that wintered here in 879-880 is the band that 'sat at Fulham by the Thames', which the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle 879-880 (Ingram 1823, checked at avalon.law.yale.edu/medieval/ang09.asp) keeps apart from the army Alfred beat. Andoverpis has no rampart before about 900 (places/andoverpis.json; Bellens 2021), so in these years it is a landing with a church. In the London toll rules the emperor's men come after the men of Flanders (chronicle_793.json 1000-london-tolls). No paper north of the Alps: charters.

Not opened, and nothing rests on them alone: Walahfrid Strabo's preface to the Life of Charles and Alcuin's verses on Einhard's small stature; the Miracles of Bavo (the man of the port carried to Rouen), known here through Verhulst
